utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Sarah Clanton; Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; legal interns, Lucy Jones, Katherine Davis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just before I begin, though, one small, little housekeeping matter. For the record, what is now in evidence as Exhibit P2310, should be linked to 65 ter number 4774.3. Currently it is linked to 65 ter 4774. And so just to add the .3 to the 65 ter number. And we've consulted with the Registrar about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, yes, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we continue from yesterday, I'd like to actually go back to a few things that you said today -- or excuse me, yesterday, or previously during the course of your cross-examination. And the first of these is at page 10071 of the transcript, and I was asking you about the time of the events in late 1991. I was asking whether you knew, among other things, that Arkan was a criminal. And you said in answer: "You're asking me if I knew whether he was a criminal, and I told you that I didn't know at the time ..." Mr. Hadzic, is it possible that you said something differently to Vladimir Dzuro during the course of your suspect interview and at that time you said that you actually knew that he was wanted by Interpol and was a criminal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what period I discussed with Mr. Dzuro and what you had in mind. I told you that when I first met him, I didn't know that he was a criminal. I didn't know anything about him. And since in the country where I resided, there were no criminal reports against him, he had never been arrested, for me it was enough, I did not have any possibility to run a check on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1084. This is 65 ter 04974.03K. And this is English page 25 -- sorry, 32 of the English, 25 of the B/C/S and we'll just play this short video-clip when the interpreters tell us that they've got it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hadzic, if you're not able to hear it, let us know and we'll stop and start again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Arkan went into -- launched military operations in a disciplined manner, regardless of what you say and which is true that he was wanted by Interpol, that he was a criminal, and that a warrant for his arrest had been issued."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you knew, Mr. Hadzic, at the time he was involved in military operations, despite your opinion that he operating or acting in a disciplined manner, you did know at the time, at that time in 1991 and during the conflict, that he was a wanted criminal by Interpol. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously that's not the case. This is a play on words, it seems. When Mr. Dzuro asked me, I knew then. When he first arrived with the Serbian police as a member of the Serbian state, i.e., a member of the federal state, I could not vet him. Later on, I heard rumours that he was wanted by the Interpol. I don't know whether Serbia had to comply with the Interpol's demands and why he wasn't arrested by the authorities of the state where he resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Another item from yesterday, Mr. Hadzic, going now to page 10116 of the transcript, I was asking you about the appointment of Mr. Petrovic to be the minister of information for your government. I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, could you give us a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, if you're moving on to another line of questions this -- the last exchange between yourself and the witness, what -- I'm not sure about and perhaps either the answer or the question was -- well, certainly the -- the -- what I'm left with is not very clear. But, Mr. Hadzic, do I understand your testimony to be that back in 1991 you didn't know that Arkan was wanted by Interpol, et cetera, however, at the time of the interview with Mr. Dzuro, you did know? My question is: When did you learn that Arkan was a criminal, that he was wanted by Interpol?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood this first part well. In 2002, I told Mr. Dzuro that I'd -- I knew that when I was talking to him. As for the precise time when I learned that, I can't remember exactly when that was, but certainly around the time when Arkan became a well known media personality, when they talked about him, when foreign journalists came, even an Australian MP came to visit him as well, and there was -- a lot of controversy surrounded him. They said he was a colonel of the SFRY State Security, that he was a criminal, somebody whose job was to kill all over Europe. That's what I heard. And it was only later, perhaps in 95-96 that I heard that he had also robbed banks, in the Netherlands or Sweden. I'm not sure where. After 1991, I heard a lot of controversial stories, but I have never heard that a final judgement of conviction was passed against him. I don't remember learning that, nor did anyone tell me that officially. I never received that either from Interpol or any other organisation, or any police in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to briefly follow up on it, Mr. Hadzic, perhaps I could have done a better job of trying to set the time-frame, because in your response to my question you actually said that: Later on I heard rumours that he was wanted by Interpol. Can we agree that by the time of his wedding in early 1995, Mr. Raznjatovic was a well-known figure in the media, and certainly by the time of his wedding in 1995 you would have been aware of all of the controversy, if I can put it that way, that swirled around Arkan and his reputation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time those stories already existed, and I also heard that Arkan had been arrested in Croatia and released. And I thought Croatia was a state - now it's even a member of the European Union - if they were serious in this shape, there was a strong indications that he had indeed committed a crime. Croatia as a signatory of Interpol would have extradited him to the countries that issued a warrant against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in your answer to Judge Hall's question, you made a reference to the Australian consul who came to visit him. Are you referring now to the footage that we looked at when the gentleman from Australia came to the training centre and then also met with you and Arkan? We showed you to that at the beginning of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that he was a consul; he was a MP in the Australian parliament. He visited Arkan; Arkan was his host. I received the gentleman independently of that, and Arkan was his escort during that visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now to move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You will have a date for that visit, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The visit of the Australian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. I -- we have it as January 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I asked you yesterday a question about Mr. Petrovic. I said: "You selected Mr. Petrovic and put him forward to be information minister of your government; isn't that correct?" And you said: "In the formal sense, yes. But it was not my independent decision. It was also a result of the proposal of the rest of those who were at the meeting, president of the Assembly, Koncarevic, some others with whom we'd agreed about. But the assembly of SBWS was the one that made its decision on their appointment." Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you there, Mr. Hadzic, and maybe it's something that just needs to be clarified, but one could get the impression that you were minimising the role that you played and the -- the extent to which you had the ability and the authority to select those who would be members of your government. The fact is that you selected those members of the government and 100 per cent, all of the people that you selected, were in fact approved by the assembly. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In formal term, this is the truth, but in practical terms it is not. But it is very interesting to hear you say that I tried to minimise my role. I had an opportunity to say to the Trial Chamber that I cannot minimise it -- to the extent that it was really minimal. It was ten times less significant than it may seem now, as I am telling you this. At that time I did not have a telephone. I didn't have a car. I didn't have any possibility to contact anybody. I could only use the courier services or acquaintances in order to send messages to people to come to Dalj because I was waiting for them and then wait to see whether they would turn up or not. At the time I didn't even have a place where I could eat. And this is the truth of the matter. Now, whether this was minimum or maximum, I leave it to you to be the judge of that. But this is how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's just take a look at what you said about this when Mr. Dzuro asked you about it in 2002. That would be tab 1083, 65 ter 04974.02 and the letter N, for Nancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we know why the text on the screen from the interview of Mr. Hadzic is redacted in some parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The reason for that is that it can take the interpreters directly to the part that corresponds to the clip. Now the Defence have obviously the complete unredacted version. This is done in order to guide the interpreters. It's done in other cases as well. This is the practice in other trials. If they don't like it, we can -- we can change it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that these parts could be highlighted and not -- not blacked. Not in black, because I don't know -- as far as I know it is a public document. And could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could be seen on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I must say, I, for myself, wouldn't think that we get on the screen the document that is -- I mean, the -- the version of the document that is only there for the booth. So I would indeed prefer to have the real document rather than the document that is there to help the booth with the translation of the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll make the adjustment, Mr. President. And, in any event, we're just running the video so we can all hear what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: "Vladimir Dzuro: Yeah. If I may return to the government of Selo, I mean who - you appointed those ministers, who -- did somebody have to approve it -- the appointment? "Goran Hadzic: [Interpretation] Yes, the Grand National -- the Grand People's Assembly -- the Grand National Assembly. "Vladimir Dzuro: And did they actually approve those ministers? "Goran Hadzic: [Interpretation] Yes, it did with 100 per cent certainty. I just now cannot remember when this was done. I believe it's logical that this took place somewhere in September, because later we had regular assembly sessions."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And before I come back to you, let's just go ahead also to what you said in the Dokmanovic case. This is 65 ter 02320. And this would be for the Registrar, this is not a video-clip. This is the testimony from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, do we still have to be in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- I don't know why we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We are not in private session so we don't take that signal into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I see, actually, we do have -- we did manage to get the video from Mr. Hadzic's testimony in the Dokmanovic case on this point, and so with the Chamber's permission, we'll run that. This would be 65 ter 2320.1. And this is at pages 3077 to 3078 of the Dokmanovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Q. How did Mr. Dokmanovic become to be minister of agriculture? "A. Slavko Dokmanovic was a very honourable man, and, as you know, he was and still is. He had graduated from the school of agriculture. He was nearby. I was able to appoint him. I appointed him as such and politically, this also strictly corresponded to our requirements because he was a very good political decision. "Q. Was he easily elected or were there those Serbs who did not want to elect him? "A. With all the reasonable Serbs, the choice was okay, but there were very few of such people. Most extremists attacked him, and I had a lot of problems and I had to use all of my authority to have Slavko appointed as minister."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadzic, what you said there and this was when you were a Defence witness for Mr. Dokmanovic, is that in fact you had authority and you exercised your authority in order to put those people into your government whom you wanted and so it wasn't quite as -- well, you in fact did minimise your evidence on this, and you've continued to do so. It's basically your decision. You consulted with others, and the ones you selected were approved. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we have gone in two completely different directions with regard to your conclusions and my answers. Obviously I didn't understand your question. When I spoke about my minimum role, I meant the role of my government and my possibility to work. When it comes to the appointment of ministers who played a role, the situation is very clear. I told you that I had two basic views: One was professional; the other was territorial. And apart from my proposals there are also proposals from local communes and professional associations that had a say. Those are two completely separate things. As for my minimum role and my possibilities to work, that's what I had in mind. It is absolutely irrelevant how able I was to appoint ministers whose names I personally put forward, such as Slavko Dokmanovic, or some others proposed by the local communes of Borovo Selo or Trpinja. Those are two different things. I suppose I didn't understand you well. My proposal to appoint Dokmanovic was as valid as the proposal that came from a local commune, but we were all obviously talking at cross-purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Interpreters are asking if you could slow down a bit, Mr. Hadzic. Maybe we were not understanding each other. I'm going to suggest to you that you consulted. There were criteria for selection. It's not an unusual thing. You made the selection and 100 per cent of your selections were approved by the -- [Technical difficulty]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It will make a minute or two, Mr. Stringer, to solve the problem. Could the court reporter adjust the last sentence of mine. It looks a little bit stupid the way it is now. It will take a minute or two, Mr. Stringer, to solve the problem. Thank you. I think we are back in business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that right? Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, with the interruption there, let me just try to start again. I'm not asking you about the extent to which you had the supplies, the paper, or the phones, or the cars in order to function as a government. I'm asking you about the manner in which the ministers were selected and appointed. And can we agree, sir, that in appointing your minister, you consulted with others - there were criteria - you made the decision, and 100% of the ministers whom you chose were in fact approved by the Great National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Great National Assembly approving their appointments, that is not in dispute. I said so to Mr. Dzuro and we all know about it here. It could not have been any other way. I have explained that as regards the procedural parts I suggested to the national assembly to have those ministers appointed. I have explained the procedure before the appointment as such. Some people were proposed by Dalj, others from Borovo Selo, and we also got some from Serbia such as the minister for urban planning and construction and the minister of finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's a simple question, Mr. Hadzic. All of those whom you proposed were approved. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is asked an answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I -- I disagree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's a simple question, Mr. Hadzic. All of those whom you proposed were approved. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a very simple question but it contains two parts: In terms of procedure, all of the ministers I proposed were accepted by the assembly; as for the other part, I explained the procedure of nomination and appointment. It had to come formally from me because I was the prime minister designate. In that sense, your assertion would be fine. But I did explain to you the factual situation of the proposals and the way they were made. So procedurally your logic is correct, but factually it is flawed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I asked you questions yesterday about the Serbian National Council, and I'm looking now at pages 10084, -85 of the transcript, also 10090. On 10085, I was suggesting to you that Mr. Petrovic as spokesperson of the SNC was actually articulating what was the platform and the objective of the SNC on establishing a line of separation between Croatian and Serbian people and facilitating population movement. At the time, we were looking that exhibit, 65 ter 1939.4, which you said you didn't know about. And, again, yesterday you said is -- is -- is -- "That's not correct. This is what Ilija Petrovic was talking about. I had no idea about it." Moving down, same page, 10085, line 15, you said that you reluctantly agreed to attend meetings of the SNC but this was not something that was ever discussed. Page 10090, I asked: "Did the SNC have territorial aspirations?" You said: This was never discussed at meetings. I saw that when I came here in the book, Petrovic's book, and that was the first time that I heard the geographic term "Moslavina." To tell you the truth, I don't even know today exactly what this territory is, Moslavina." You remember that testimony from yesterday, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 999, which is P1956. This is video footage. And we'll wait for the interpreters. We'll start on page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Also page 1 of the B/C/S. And we'll let this run for 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: Ilija Petrovic, member of the National Council; Ilija Koncarevic, secretary general of the Serbian National Council; Pero Matic, professor from Beli Manastir; Slavko Dokmanovic, chairman of the municipal assembly of Vukovar; Goran Hadzic, chairman of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party Vukovar and a member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party Knin; and Caslav Ocic from Dalj. The Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was formed this year in Sidski Banovci on Orthodox Christmas."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, are you able to recognise this at all, this television programme that you and the others appeared on? Does this ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that CD-ROM with the other material here. That's when I saw it. But, other than that, I don't particularly recall this broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It refers to the establishment or the formation of the Serbian National Council for SBWS on Orthodox Christmas. That's consistent with what you've told us already. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th of January, 1991. That is when the Serbian National Council was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And here, according to the anchor anyway, at this point Koncarevic and Petrovic are going public with their membership in the SNC. They were both introduced as members of the SNC. You were not. That's why I'm making the distinction.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably so. I didn't observe that in the footage, but I wasn't paying attention to it. In any case, I think that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could then move forward to the second clip. Thirty-eight seconds, 37 to -- 38 minutes, 37 seconds, to 40 minutes, 12. This is page 18 of the English translation, pages 16 to 17 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booth has it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: Mr. Hadzic, do you believe that a civilised separation Mr. Ocic was talking about is possible? "Goran Hadzic: I'm an optimist by nature and I thought it was possible, this peaceful co-existence, as they call it. However, I categorically think that peaceful co-existence is not possible following these recent incidents and under these circumstances. This should be considered at the level of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, a peaceful separation should be considered. I am not for bloodshed. That is the last thing that should happen. But can you imagine the life of the people in Croatia as described by Dr. Ocic? For example, after these incidents that were shown on TV, people took to the streets unarmed at night, they were not patrolling. We were just safe-guarding our houses, or villages. Police came and the next day there was this policeman who was taking down the names. He is a Serb. It is not his fault that he was born a Serb but he does not feel as one. He was taking down the names of those who walked the street quietly on minus five and did not sleep. We were very glad he was doing this. You can imagine our lives. And that is why we decided at the last evening's Municipal Board meeting we will organise a protest rally in Vukovar, in the centre of Vukovar, 12.00 Saturday, firstly to support the measures of the Presidency, but it will also be a protest against measures of the YU Presidency not being implemented strongly enough, because the weapons that have been distributed to civilians are not handed over and the army needs to have control of it. What good is it to us if it is handed over when it can soon be given back to the same people who had handed it over."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, there's a reference there to a Dr. Ocic. Could you tell the Chamber just briefly who that person is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Caslav Ocic is a Serb from Dalj. He hails from Dalj. He was a full professor at the school of economics in Belgrade, and, to date, he is a full member of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences. In the SBWS government, he was the minister of foreign affairs. It is when the government was established a few months after this broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in terms of the time of this broadcast, you've referred to organising a rally in Vukovar on this coming Saturday. That's what you said in this clip we just saw. Does that help you recall or does that tell you what would be the time-frame in which you were appearing on this television show?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is easy to know the date because as for the rally which took place in Vukovar now I heard that it was on Saturday, and you referred previously to a news article. This broadcast had to do with information we received on Croatia's arming, and I simply expressed a concern harboured by the Serb people following that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would this television broadcast have been taking place in January or February 1991? It's referring to the establishment of the SNC. Koncarevic and Petrovic are being identified publicly with it. That suggests that in fact we're talking about January to February, the early part of 1991. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not see eye to eye on many issues here, but quite surprisingly, I agree on this one with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we know about the concerns. We understand the concerns that you -- and -- you shared with the others concerning the events in Croatia, the arming of the population that you were aware of. But what you've said here, as of January or February 1993 -- sorry, 1991, you've already reached the point or the view that a peaceful co-existence was no longer possible. Is that how you saw it as of January, February, 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously you were not either listening carefully to what I said or you are distorting facts intentionally. I said that no co-existence was possible under those conditions, and we asked for the assistance of the Presidency to have the circumstances changed, to have the arms withdrawn. And given those conditions, I said I was an optimist and in favour of co-existence. But under the conditions, when 80,000 automatic rifles have been distributed to our neighbours, consider it yourself and tell us whether co-existence is possible. If a party distributes thousands of rifles to members of a single ethnic group, well, what then?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer -- sorry, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I noticed that Mr. Hadzic mentioned two times "80.000" of rifles. In line 24, it was said "70.000." And in the line -- line 25, just "thousands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, could you confirm that with Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you've heard the exchange. Could you say again how many automatic rifles were distributed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the batch that was imported from Hungary contained 80.000. It was broadcast on TV. But there probably was more except that the army did not have that other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And going back to your previous answer, you said: "We asked for the assistance of the Presidency to have the circumstances changed." And just to be clear, we're talking about the Presidency of the SFRY, not the Presidency of Croatia, for example?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the SFRY Presidency. I also said that we were going to attend a rally in support of the Presidency to provide our support to the measures they proposed but did not implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could please go to another clip from this. This is at 24 minutes, 46, until 25 minutes, 39. Page 12 English, page 11 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this one, Mr. Hadzic, I believe you identified this gentleman yesterday we see on the screen. This is Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And here he is asked about if there's some -- if there's no more Yugoslavia and then what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so, in any event, let's -- let's start this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Serbian people, as it seems, will have to take a very firm position in that moment and commence unification into one joint state which I have been calling Serbian country for about half a year now. Serbian country singular, not Serbian countries, as some might say, because then every territory that would join this new Serbian state at some point, would have a possibility to say I'm out of here now as I'm only one of the territories of this state, once the worst is over. Therefore, a clear definition of Serbian state borders should be defined right from the beginning."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then let's play the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then I'll come back to you with some questions Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next one is at 51 minutes, 54, to 53 minutes, 14, of this exhibit, 1956. Page 24 English, page 23 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: As so as we bring this evening's broadcast to an end, let us just ask Mr. Koncarevic, secretary general of the Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, how do you see -- what is the solution for Serbs in Croatia? "Ilija Koncarevic: I'm somewhat limited by the views of the Serbian National Council in this evening's broadcast. We have today adopted a position as regards the solution to this problem that we shall forward to the Presidency. There is disputed and undisputed territory in Croatia. The undisputed territory is the territory where Croats were the ethnic majority before the beginning of World War I. The undisputed, that is disputable territory, is the one in Krajina and Western Srem, Baranja, Slavonia, and Moslavina. We propose that Yugoslav Presidencies suspend the authority of the Croatian parliament and Croatian leadership in all territories where Serbian people live. This is because elementary human rights of Serbian people have been jeopardised and one has the elementary right to live. This right has been threatened."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, a few minutes ago in answering one of my questions, you raised, you said - this is at page 17, line 22: "We asked for the assistance of the Presidency to have the circumstances changed, to have the arms withdrawn." Now, what Mr. Koncarevic has just referred to here is the same thing. True? He is referring also to an appeal or a request to be directed to the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I said. As for Koncarevic's words, I do not wish to provide any particular interpretation of it. We could all hear what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. My question is that the request to the SFRY Presidency, the Presidency that he refers to here, is the same request that you had in mind a couple of minutes ago when you answered my previous question. True?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It should be clarified whether the same request or to the same organ. Or if it is the same request, I would ask for the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 1939.04, please. It is tab number -- I apologise, Mr. President. I'm going to need a second to find the tab number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to -- while that's coming up in responding to counsel's objection, the organ that I'm talking about here is the Presidency of the SFRY. That's the only one that I've asked about, and that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we looked at this yesterday. You said you didn't know anything about it. I'd like to take another look at it now based upon the remarks that we've seen from the television programme. On the television programme, Mr. Koncarevic refers to disputable and indisputable territory in Croatia. Would you agree with me, sir, that what he is describing there actually corresponds quite nicely with paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 of the document that's now in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what he and Koncarevic wrote about in the document. Sorry, he and Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And when he says, "the SNC today adopted a position as regards the solution to this problem that we shall forward to the Presidency," he is referring to this document. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I said what my position was and what my thoughts were on what the Presidency had to be told. It had to do with the problem of the Croatian people arming themselves and that is why there was the rally in Vukovar. As for Koncarevic and Petrovic, they lived in Serbia and they did not have the same problems I did and the problems my family had living in Croatia. As for their political talk and position, I did not get involved in it. They were their personal opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, you shared their opinions, Mr. Hadzic. And as you just said a few minutes ago in your testimony, quite spontaneously and on your own, "We asked for the assistance of the Presidency." The fact is what you were referring to is this very document. True?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did he say that, that he referred to this document? May we see that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not claiming the witness referred to the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Stringer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Should I say the -- give you the question again, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. Repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your last answer you had said: "As for their political talk and position, I did not get involved in it. They were their personal opinions." And then my question was: "Well, in fact you shared their opinions, Mr. Hadzic. And as you just said a few minutes ago in your testimony, quite spontaneously and on your own, you asked for the assistance of the Presidency" -- sorry. You said, "We asked for the assistance of the Presidency." And what you're referring to there is this request that's in this document that's referred to by Koncarevic on the television show. It's the same request; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. I didn't know about that request and that letter. I said then very clearly, clearly and spontaneously, that we asked for the Presidency's help for everybody to disarm. When I said "everybody," I meant that -- I meant by that Croatia, which had armed itself, but also those Serbs who had obtained arms, so that life together would be possible. I meant that we would live normally and that I was an optimist and in favour of coexistence. As for your conclusions here, they have nothing to do with what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In his remarks, Mr. Koncarevic also proposes that the Yugoslav Presidency suspend the authority of the Croatian Sabor. And we see that in fact that request or demand is contained in this document at paragraph 2, line 2, that goes to the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can repeat it for the tenth time now that I don't know anything about that document. I'm seeing it now for the first time. Actually, I saw it for the first time when I received Petrovic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But on the 3rd of February, 1991, the date of this document, you were a member of the Serbian National Council; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member as of January the 7th, but I didn't have any meetings between January 7th and February 3rd, in order to reach any decisions on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, actually, you're meeting with the gentlemen here publicly and on television. You're hearing their views. You knew precisely what the views of the Serbian National Council were as they've just been set out by Messrs. Petrovic and Koncarevic. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You heard the official anchor announce me as the president of the Social Democratic Party of the municipality of Vukovar and a member of the council, and that is why -- at the time I was representing the views of the party as well as the Serbian people, my friends and neighbours, who lived there. I did not get involved in high-ranking politics or the historical rights of either peoples, which is what Petrovic and Koncarevic were talking about. And to tell you most sincerely, even now I don't know what they referred to, these historical events, which I never actually even later felt necessary to look up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we again tender 65 ter 1939.04. We recognise that the witness won't agree that he knows anything about it or otherwise associate himself with it. But we feel that in the video footage, Petrovic and Koncarevic have quite clearly authenticated the document. The document corresponds completely to Koncarevic's statements in particular. They are both members the SNC. Mr. Hadzic is a member of the SNC. In our view, they are clearly setting out what is the policy, the objective of the SNC as set out in this document, and we think that it's sufficiently relevant and authentic to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object again. There is no foundation to -- to admit this document into evidence because the witness doesn't know anything about this particular document. He's confronted with it and it is in the transcript, but it is not reason for -- to -- to admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3214. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1005, which is P53. This is a video. And we'll wait for the interpreters to tell us when they're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Brothers and sisters, I greet you with our tradition greeting, God help us all. May God help you. As a president of the Municipal Board which you belong to, it is my duty to say something about our Vukovar Municipal Board, even though there are many topics we're going to discuss later on. Our party was established on 10th June last year in Vukovar and 19 boards have been established since then. Today the party has 21 boards. And I congratulate you on establishing your two. We have faced many problems in our party. You are familiar with them and you know who caused them. However, we managed to get over them. And we should thank or current leadership for uniting us and helping us achieve unity. We are stronger and united now. As a people, we have never looked to God, not left, not right. We always knew that we were stronger together and we have relied on that. And that's why we always sang that song, We are stronger together. I would like to tell you now something about the programme and what we discussed at the beginning. As you know, present at our rallies, our main goal was united Yugoslavia, united people's army. These are our goals even today. We have remained on the path of Saint Sava, and I wish you all the best for this holiday today. As a great Serbian academician Matija Betkovic would say, Saint Sava walked the road and everyone barked at him. But let's for get that, let's follow his road. I would rather say a few words about our current problems because I believe it is not the time for big speeches. It is time for work. We Serbs in Croatia are free-thinking democrats by our own conviction. We even had radicals before the war here, but where are we now? We have found ourselves in a situation where we have to divide into two parties due to the politics of one nation. To divide into Serbs and Croats, for us as a people, it comes as a shock. We are not nationalists. Our views are boarder but we have to accept this as a fact and organise ourselves. I believe and I am sure that everyone who watched TV two nights ago felt just like I did. This is how I am thinking. Not even 80.000 Serbs can we manage to find in the world and persuade them to talk badly about other people. And others have been given 80.000 machine-guns and are keeping them so that they could use them against us. This is ridiculous. 1941 happened. 1945 happened. Then 1971. And then we thought, we would forgive them. It would not happen again. But I'm telling you now, very responsibly, if the Croatian people do not renounce their Ustashas publicly, for the first time since 1941, we will propose through our Serbian National Council to cut all ties between Serbs and Croats. Our perphidious policy led since the 1850s since the time of Ante Starcevic has reached final stage now. They were not so perphidious. Had they led their perphidious policy for another couple of years, the Serb people would not have managed to unite. They can do nothing to us now on a regional legal, on a republican and federal level. They are facing problem. Let me tell you why: Because we are democratic. We have thought about things that they had said and we thought whether or not they really meant it. However, I thank them for that. We're united and there will be no division within the party. We understood that people should talk but there can be no dialogue with them. I would not talk about this anymore. I would like to invite you to join the Social Democratic Party. You don't have to become members of the party but just follow its policy and participate in its activities. Three days ago, we had a meeting in Trpinja with intellectuals. Well, we call them intellectuals but, actually, they were businessmen of the Vukovar municipality. We expected -- we invited 50 or 60 of them but some 200 of them turned up. It means that people who had not been organised before realised where they belong. We told them that a huge number of Serbian people do not belong to the Social Democratic Party, many of them belong to the Social Democratic Party, but the remaining irrelevant part of them ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Text unclear, interpreter notes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... here I have it in my pocket. I have prepared some conclusions that were reached at that meeting, but I'd rather not read them to you. It will be published in all newspapers tomorrow or the day after. I would just like to tell you a few words of what the conclusions were. It was concluded ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Text unclear, interpreter notes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... support of the Vukovar municipality for the recognition of the Serbian National Council. More importantly, it was decided that the board of representatives for the protection of Serbian national interest should be established within the Vukovar Municipal Assembly. We do represent the Social Democratic Party, but, above all, we have interests of the Serbian people in mind. I beg you, well, I'm not begging you, but I ask you to think about the interests of the Serbian people before anything else. I would like to finish this speech with the words: God help us, and he will."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, at the beginning of the video, not at the beginning but at -- an earlier part, you make a reference to Saint Sava and wishing all of those people there all the best for this holiday today. Is that Saint Sava Day which I believe falls in late January?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this is -- is it the 27th of January, 1991, when this speech took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we heard in this speech two references to the Serbian National Council. I suggest to you, sir, that you were clearly supporting and advocating the Serbian National Council as a body through which you were acting. Isn't it true that in late January of 1991 you were participating and advocating the Serbian National Council to other Serbs in the region?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian National Council was founded in early January, so there was no need for me to speak anything against it in late January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact in referring to it, you referred to it as "our Serbian National Council." Mr. Hadzic, you knew precisely what the Serbian National Council stood for, and you were participating and advocating that it act on the behalf of all Serbs. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for your assertion that I knew what it was standing for, it is correct, and that is what I said both I and the Serbian National Council stood for, but that is not what you are claiming as regards this letter by Ilija Petrovic, which I did not even know about. It's not the same thing. I still think, and I also thought then, that the Serbian National Council was in favour of preserving the interests of the Serbian people. We are a people who went through genocide in World War II, and I believed that after this, if you understood it from my speech, that at the time it was announced that Croatia had armed itself with 80.000 automatic rifles, and this was a consequence of that. And for that reason, I would like to ask you to keep that in mind and keep that context in mind when you are discussing this particular footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were on the television programme with Messrs. Petrovic and Koncarevic, you were a member of the Serbian National Council at the time of the television conversation, and you heard Koncarevic articulating very clearly what the SNC's objectives were. So you knew fully what its objectives were. You knew fully what the SNC was about, as set out on the television show by Koncarevic, as well as in this document that was sent to the SFRY Presidency in early February.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I understood Koncarevic's speech as something that was personal, and we were there, each of us, in our private capacity, as individuals. What we should keep in mind here is that this was an attempt here at peaceful resolution of the problem without war and without any suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please go back to the clip of Koncarevic. Again, it's tab 999, P1956. It's at 51 minutes, 54. Page 24 of the English, 23 of the B/C/S. It's my last question on this, Mr. President, and I'll move on. We'll wait for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we're ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: And so as we bring this evening's broadcast to an end, let us just ask Mr. Koncarevic, secretary general of the Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, how do you see -- what is the solution for Serbs in Croatia? "Ilija Koncarevic: I am somewhat limited by the views of the Serbian National Council in this evening's broadcast. We have today adopted a position as regards the solution to this problem that we shall forward to the Presidency. There is disputable and indisputable territory in Croatia. The indisputable territory is the territory where the Croats were an ethnic majority before the beginning of World War I."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, what Mr. Koncarevic makes clear here is that he is not expressing his personal views. He is referring expressly to the views of the Serbian National Council. That's my suggestion. He says: "I'm somewhat limited by the views of the Serbian National Council in this evenings's broadcast. We have today adopted a position ..." So he is not speaking about his personal views. He's in fact expressing the policy of the SNC of which you are a member; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. That is not correct. We did not even meet that day. Mr. Koncarevic here is trying to increase the reputation of the Serbian National Council which was just being established, so he gave himself some more importance, and it was obvious to me. It may seem strange to you now, but what he was saying is that he now had an organisation to back him, which, at that time, was just in the process of being established, so it wasn't even meeting at the time. I could have jumped up and slapped him. But I wasn't his father or instructor to tell him that he was lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, actually as it turned out, Mr. Koncarevic, who we see here on the screen, turned out to be the president of the Great National Assembly of the SBWS when it began issuing laws in September of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if the witness could repeat his last sentence. Here in transcript state: "But I wasn't his father or any figure who could be able to tell him that he was lying." I think that he said something else in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, could you ask the witness to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you please do so, Mr. Hadzic. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said I wasn't his father or his instructor, a person bringing him up. The other thing was, that I could have jumped up and slapped him and told him he was lying. I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You just asserted that what Mr. Koncarevic was doing was trying to increase the reputation of the Serbian National Council. In fact, that's exactly what you were doing when you gave the speech that we just saw on Saint Sava Day in which you were out there advocating and telling people what the SNC was going to do for them. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's why the Serbian National Council was founded, to take care of the overall interests of the Serbian people, and for us not to permit for the worst thing to happen to us, what I referred to. In history this is something that is well-known. It was supposed to be a non-party, above-party organisation, to represent all Serbs, and not only the members of the Serbian Democratic Party, at least that's how I understood it when I was there at that founding assembly. It was supposed to be an umbrella organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a couple of minutes early, but I'm going to be making a big change in topic at this point, so it may be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. We'll take the first break. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can please have tab 388. This is L1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we're going to go back to some of the laws that were in the Official Gazettes of the SBWS as we were doing yesterday at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'd -- I asked that we go first -- or next, I should say, to the Law on the Government of the Serb District of the SBWS which is at page 29 of the English, and at the moment I do not have a B/C/S page reference to give to the Registrar. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I don't want to spend too much time on this, Mr. Hadzic, but at Article 1 there, we see -- well, let me ask you this first: This is passed on 9th of October, 1991. I think the ones we discussed yesterday were passed on the 25th of September. This law passed at the 3rd Session on the 9th of October, 1991. Do you know where that government session would have been held?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation I got was "the government," whereas on the document, I can see the word "assembly." I believe that you misspoke. Did you mean the government or actually the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It may be that you're looking at a different law than -- than I'm looking at. I'm looking at the Law on the Government of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It is ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But your question was about when that government session took place. However, I can see in the document that it was an assembly session on the 9th of October. So I suppose that your question should be where the assembly session took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're right, I misspoke. Assembly session. Was that in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that all the assembly sessions were held in Beli Manastir, so this one should not have been an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And according to this law, then, the government of the SBWS - this is Article 1 - as the organ of executive authority shall carry out the duties as specified by the constitutional law and shall be responsible for the Great National Assembly for the discharge of such duties. Mr. Hadzic, just so we're clear, so you, as prime minister, were the head of the executive part of the government, that is, the government -- the part that was responsible for carrying out the duties set out in the -- in the law?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was meant. However, I have to emphasise that all of this had been prepared for some normal time, for peacetime. In that area, throughout 1991, we had a military administration and that continued in 1992. Those decisions were prepared for the moment when civilian authorities would be able to take over in peacetime. However, all of these decisions were passed during the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in Article 2, then we see that the government is to conduct the policy of the SBWS and that in item 3 it had the power to adopt decrees, decisions, and other acts for enforcing the laws. You recall, Mr. Hadzic, that in fact during this period, 1991 included, you actually did adopt decrees, decision, the government did, pursuant to Article 2 here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the government did make proposals and adopted some things, but most of the laws were adopted by the assembly, and the assembly was the only body that was allowed to pass any laws because it was the legislative body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, tell us what was the difference between the law passed by the Great National Assembly in a decree or decision here that is referred to in item 3? Can you give an example of something the government could adopt a decree or decision about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember a single case. There were such cases. I can't remember them. Those were the so-called decree laws, but I can't remember any one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You signed off on decisions appointing people to positions, for example, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could do that only based on the government's decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question was: You signed off on decisions appointing people to positions. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. But I do think that I signed off every government's decision or everything that was in keeping with the government's decisions. I can't remember that I signed anything independently of my own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next law in the Gazette is the Law on Measures in the state of emergency and we're going to skip over that one. I'm going to skip over that one, going to skip over the Law on Courts, and we're going to go to the decision on the Territorial Defence of the SBWS joining SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is page 62 of the English, 20 of -- page 20 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated the 10th of October, 1991. And we see in Article 1 that the Territorial Defence of the SBWS is hereby joining with SFRY armed forces and becoming part of it. Article 2: "The government of the Serb District of SBWS is authorised to take all measures necessary to execute this decision, in co-operation with the Federal Secretariat of National Defence." Mr. Hadzic, can we agree that Article 2, the reference to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, is indeed the federal body of the SFRY, the SFRY Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time we were part of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, really, this decision here is -- is simply doing what the SFRY -- let me start again. The decision is making clear what really the SFRY law already provides, which is that the Territorial Defence is a part of the SFRY armed forces under the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was under the law. The armed forces consisted of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. In wartime, they were one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago, Mr. Hadzic, I asked you about appointments. I do want to step off this document for a few moments and ask you something related to appointments but for a different time-period. In your testimony on direct examination, on the 8th of July, transcript page 9517, you were shown an exhibit, D117. I believe it was the text of a -- of a news article related to the appointment of Ilija Kojic as the commander of the Territorial Defence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then at page 9519 of the transcript, you said that Janko Milakovic was elected at the proposal of Ilija Kojic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Ilija Kojic suggested that Janko Milakovic should be appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I think that the name of -- okay. Okay. It is corrected. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologise. Let's skip over tab 22, which was D117, that's the document I just asked Mr. Hadzic about, and move to tab 753. 65 ter 1939.14.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As that's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, this is one of the documents we reproduced from Mr. Petrovic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry. This should be 65 ter 1939.14. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Hadzic, that it was -- it was you as chairman of the -- what this document says National Council of Serbs that you signed off on the appointment to establish a Territorial Defence Staff on the 14th of July and that Mr. Kojic was, at that time, appointed as commander of the Territorial Defence Staff. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he was both proposed and appointed, but I don't remember having signed anything. I may have, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As of this time - 14th of July, 1991 - you were the chairman or the president of the SNC, the Serb National Council; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally. I was appointed on the 26th of June in Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in that capacity on this day, you appointed Mr. Kojic to be the commander of the TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbian National Council that appointed him. I was nothing more than its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3215. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could now have tab 754, which is 65 ter number 1939.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at roughly the same time here, mid-July 1991, did -- well, was Mr. Milakovic here, as indicated, appointed as the secretary of the regional secretariat of the interior called the SUP and that was also done through you and the SNC?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the SNC did that. But I don't remember having signed that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But in terms of what's indicated in the document here, you don't disagree with this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I need to see what's in it. I know that Janko Milakovic was appointed as the SUP secretary but I don't remember that the decision was passed at the assembly session. Also I don't remember that I signed the document to that effect but I know that he was appointed and that he had been put forward by Ilija Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, actually, this document is dated as the -- the same day, the 14th of July, that the Kojic document is -- the Kojic appointment that we just saw. The Milakovic is done through the SNC then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I should have thought so, yes. I'm confused by the -- by what he said and that he was nominated by somebody called Ante. I don't know any such person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Hadzic. I'm not seeing what you're -- what you're referring to there, Ante?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we should move to the private session in -- at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Hadzic, the question is simply whether as indicated here this gentleman, Mr. Milakovic, was appointed to this position, secretary of the SUP, on the 14th of July by or through the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so in here. I said the other thing as well, but that's what it says in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We would tendered that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned exhibit P3216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tab 757, please, which is 65 ter 1939.18. This is another one from the Petrovic book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As it's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, I can tell you it's 23rd of August, 1991. Proclamation of general mobilisation. And, actually -- or, I should say, and, actually, this one in the original language version appears to be above your handwritten signature. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this is my signature. But I am not denying the fact that this proclamation was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your direct examination at page 9651, you were asked if you remembered that the government of SBWS in the summer of 1991 issued a declaration on general mobilisation. And you said that you did, indeed, remember that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I explained. I said that those people had left the territory, their houses stayed behind, and some of their family members, mostly the elderly parents, they lived carefree in Serbia while their houses and their family members were supposed to be protected by their neighbours, and there was a great pressure from those neighbours, who were not happy and insisted that those people should come back and defend their own homes. I believe that you will remember that I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just for context, this is -- this is taking place about three weeks or so after the operation at Dalj in which the first of the towns was, as you would say, liberated. And so the mobilisation here is -- is going out, I would suggest, because in the weeks following the liberation of Dalj, conditions were better for people who had left to come back. Would -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had nothing to do with the liberation of Dalj. It applied to the entire territory at that moment. We met in Dalj by chance because there were adequate premises there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have tab 205, please, which is P00166.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a "Politika" article published on the 24th of August, 1991, and it's reporting on the general mobilisation. And here it says: "The government of SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem yesterday declared general mobilisation. The proclamation signed by Prime Minister Goran Hadzic reads as follows ..." and then the text.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is the same, the only difference being that this is a newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would agree with you on that, sir. My point here is what's indicated here is in fact a proclamation. The document was signed by you, and so I'd suggest that in fact, as we've seen in the earlier document, you personally issued the general mobilisation in your capacity as prime minister, as what's indicated here, even though you were prime minister-elect at the time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your assertion. I signed this as the conclusion from a meeting that I had with government members, i.e. I signed it on behalf of everybody. I don't know if this is my signature at all, but I do remember that decision on mobilisation and I explained why it had been passed. I already said that I'm not contesting this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, then we would tender 1939.18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3217. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I have just one moment, Mr. President. I apologise. Thank you. The next exhibit is tab 763, 65 ter 1939.24, again from the Petrovic book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, this is what's called: "An appeal of the defence commander for AO, Autonomous District, Baranja, Slavonia, and Western Srem last call to battle. 25th September is the last deadline for return of all men fit for combat."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we can ask the Registrar to move to the last page of it, page 5 of the English. Apologies. Page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What we see here is that this is above the name of Ilija Kojic. And my question is whether you recall this, Mr. Hadzic, that as a result of or as a follow-up to the mobilisation order that we just looked at that went out in late August, the 24th of August, there was a subsequent call on the part of Mr. Kojic, who is indicated here as defence commander of the autonomous district, for able-bodied men to return and to take part in the hostilities. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Kojic was injured and left the -- the theatre, the -- the area of SBWS in early October 1991. What was he doing during the few weeks prior to that, say, around the date of this, 22nd of September?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the candidates for minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We were given that you said, "He was one of the candidates for minister of defence" of -- and I take it that that means that --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, not one of. He was a candidate and he was actually acting minister of defence before his appointment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat the date he placed at the very end of the sentence. We did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you repeat the date that you say -- that you gave at the end of your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th of September, when the Great National Assembly sat. But even before that, it was general knowledge that he would be the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He was sort of like a minister of defence-elect, like you were the prime minister-elect, if you will?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we now please have tab 333, which is L38.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, we've -- you talked about this document already in your direct examination. These are the minutes of a government session held in Erdut on the 19th of November, 1991. And before I ask you about the document, I wanted to ask you -- you gave -- you testified in your direct examination that the secretary, who I believe was Mr. Pejakovic, who was the person who actually made the minutes, he remained in Dalj even though the government moved to Erdut at some point. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if it indicates in the upper left-hand corner here, it says, "Dalj, 20 November 1991," is that indicating that in fact Mr. Pejakovic made the minutes in Dalj on the day after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is obvious, at least to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the meeting itself occurred in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now at this meeting were yourself, Dr. Hadzic, Ilija Petrovic, other members of the government. Absent was Ilija Kojic. And then present also was Sava Stupar and Radovan Stojicic, among others. And, again, just to remind ourselves, this is the 19th of November, so the fall of Vukovar, I'd suggest, is imminent. Actually, it's already fallen on the previous day, the 18th; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And turning to page 2 of the English, the agenda is item 1 is "for the adoption of the draft Law on Temporary Territorial Organisation of the Serbian District of SBWS and temporary local administration." And then item 2 is the report on the military and political situation. And then item 3 for an activity plan. And then in the minutes there, the discussion on item 1, Mr. Susa, who was the minister of justice, briefed those present on the draft Law on Temporary Territorial Organisation. The question was raised whether or not Ilok should have the status of a municipality, and then also it was stated that because of the political situation, the seat of Osijek municipality should be temporarily located in Tenja. So what's happening here, Mr. Hadzic, is that on the day after the fall of Vukovar, the government has come together in session in order to formalise or adopt legislation that would formalise the demarkation of the SBWS territory. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exactly confirm that because I do not understand it precisely. But you can see what it is that we discussed. It was on the agenda: Current issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the issue on the agenda was to actually address the question of what would be the territory now of this district, SBWS, now that Croatian armed forces had capitulated in Vukovar. It was in your hands and the hands of the Serb side. So now it was about how to follow up on that by identifying the territory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did not happen solely because of Vukovar. What is discussed here is temporary or provisional territorial organisation. There was a question of Ilok and whether it would be a municipality and that the seat of the Osijek municipality be in Tenja, et cetera. We were not aware of the situation in Vukovar because the army was still there, and we had no access to it at the time we discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you knew that Vukovar had fallen.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole world knew, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Item 2 here on page 3 of the English has you briefing those present about the current situation from the international point of view: "Talks which had been held with the representatives of the Republic of Serbia and the Yugoslav People's Army." My first question, Mr. Hadzic, then, is: Who it that you spoke to? "Representatives of the Republic of Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as October, I was in intensive consultation with international guests from international institutions, as well as with representatives of the Republic of Serbia. At the time I had discussions with a general by the name of Slavko Jovic concerning the arrival of Blue Helmets. Before that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
