utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the last part of your answer, your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent by the Serbian President, Slobodan Milosevic, to meet with the general, Mr. Jovic. I think I've explained that during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, this says "representatives." It's in the plural. Were there other representatives of Serbia that you were in touch with during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in contact with those experts who were versed in international politics: Vasilje Krestic, Kosta Mihajlovic, Milenko Kreca, Smilja Avramov [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in terms of contacts or talks with the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago it was Major-General Slavko Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in the same paragraph, moving down a few lines, the government unanimously decided that the commander of the Territorial Defence had their full confidence and that its status had been established by the decision of the Great people's Assembly which proclaimed the units of the Territorial Defence form a part of the Yugoslav forces. So here, Mr. Hadzic, the commander of the Territorial Defence who is being referred to here is Radovan Stojicic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously we did not decide on that; we only provided our full support and he had already been imposed on us, so to say. We merely confirmed the de facto situation. We were not asked about it. However, we did say that we were not against it. Even if we had been, there would have been no point, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's different than that, Mr. Hadzic. You make it sound as though were sort of reluctantly, grudgingly having to put up with him. In fact, he was welcomed by you and he had your full support, that is, he had the full support of your government; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been so or not, but it didn't change a thing. He came as a federal representative, and he appropriated that position independent of the government will. We could agree or disagree, but we believed it to be better not to cause any trouble around that because there would have been no point, and we did not have a reason to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that the government of the SBWS had full confidence in Radovan Stojicic as its TO commander on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see in the conclusion, one might say so. But I would rather say that we could not hold a grudge against him, and there was no reason for us to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, why would you not have been happy about having him as your TO commander? Things were in disarray when he arrived. He came and sorted out your police and he came and sorted out your Territorial Defence; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. But he did all that of his own accord, without any previous arrangements with us. It is true that he did that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you happily accepted his support and his work; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how happy we were, but we had to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please go back now to L1, the Gazettes, tab 388. And now to the -- the Law on the Temporary Territorial Organisation of the Serb Region of SBWS and the Temporary Local Administration. It's at page 84 of the English; page 20 of the B/C/S at the bottom on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we were just looking at the government -- the minutes of the government meeting on the 19th of November when your justice minister, Mr. Susa, brought the draft Law on Territorial Organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't have on the screen, on the left side of the screen, the text that corresponds to the right side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry. It's page 29 of the B/C/S. Right, that's my mistake. Page 29 of the B/C/S. Again, at the bottom on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we see in the preamble, Mr. Hadzic, that this law was taken up at the fifth regular session on the 22nd of November, 1991. So it's three days after the government meeting in Erdut that we were discussing before. So the question is whether the draft law that Mr. Susa brought to the meeting of the government on the 19th of November is what we're seeing here now in the Gazette as having been adopted by the assembly three days later at its session on the 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this place here, I can presume it was so, but I cannot be 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As the justice minister, it was Mr. Susa who was, I would think, at least among those who drafted proposed legislation to be presented to the assembly for its consideration. Is that one of the roles he played?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But I think he was assisted by some experts from the federal state that we were a part of. That is to say, the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to Article 7 of this law. Page 30 of the B/C/S; 85, English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, actually, you can see in Article 6 as well, it's talking about names of existing inhabited places being changed. That's in Article 6. That they can't be changing the names until elections for the district assembly are underway. And then in Article 7 there's a reference to Executive Councils and that's what I want to ask you about here. It says: "Executive Councils of the municipalities, in agreement with the Executive Councils of the local commune, determine the names of parts of the inhabited place (street, squares) with the prior consent of the ministry authorised in matters of town planning." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us briefly: What were the Executive Councils referred to here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reference is made to the Executive Councils of municipalities and local communes. At the time, there was no possibility to set up assemblies in municipalities and local communes. Hence, the Executive Councils exercised the functions of civilian authorities both in the communes and the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then moving to Article 10, here we see setting out what in fact are or will be the municipalities in the Serb District: "The municipalities in the Serb District are Vukovar, Beli Manastir, Vinkovci, with temporary seat in Mirkovci, Dalj and Osijek, with temporary seat in Tenja." And then we see in Article 11, and it continues on for several pages, a listing of the actual villages or settlements, towns within the municipalities that fall within the territorial organisation of the SBWS. Starting with Vukovar, continuing across page 87 of the English, to Beli Manastir. Page 88, Vinkovci. Page 89, Dalj. And we don't have to look at all of those right now. We're going to look at a few of them in the moments to come. So what's happening here, Mr. Hadzic, is that this being the 22nd of November, 1991, the Serbs had achieved military control over much of the territorial that it was claiming for the Serb District. Can we first agree on that: By the 22nd of November, the Serbs had achieved military control over much of the territory that it was claiming for the Serb District?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. Military control was established by the JNA. They had their own Presidency with members who were not only Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me clarify that then. For the moment, I don't want to distinguish between military or political control, Serb military, or Serb politicians. I just simply want to see if we can agree that by the 22nd of November, the Serb side, if you will, had achieved control over much of what was claimed to be SBWS autonomous district.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree with you if, instead of the Serb side, you used the term the Yugoslav side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that. Now, looking at Article 11 here, which we're seeing Vukovar and then a number of the towns that are located in it, and keeping that in mind -- well, let's move across to the next page so the Chamber can see more of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Next page of the English. This is Beli Manastir. And then with a number of -- maybe I should ask you, Mr. Hadzic, under Beli Manastir, here just, for example, we're seeing individual locations, such as Baranjsko Petrovo Selo, Batina, Bilje, Bolman, Branjin. What are those places, towns, villages inside Beli Manastir municipality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are all villages in the Beli Manastir municipality. Beli Manastir itself a town. All of these are villages in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving across to the next page of the English, page 88, again the list of places in Beli Manastir continues. And then Vinkovci appears. And then it continues with the list of places in Vinkovci. And then on page 89, moves into Dalj. And then page 90, Osijek. Temporary seat in Tenja. So what's happening here, Mr. Hadzic, is that by virtue of this Law on Territorial Organisation, the places are being identified over which the Serbian District and its government and its legislative governmental bodies will be applying their laws and their jurisdiction in place of the Law on the Jurisdiction of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But in some future period when fighting stops and when the military administration hands over power to the civilian administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now if we could please have P01776 which is tab 394.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is, Mr. Hadzic, as it's coming up, this is the census -- the census data for these places that I want to take you to from the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we would go first to e-court page 26. That's page 26 of the e-court file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at the top there, the third entry is for Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could blow that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, what this is telling us is that according to the 1991 census, they've got 54.265 people in Beli Manastir - this is the municipality - of which 22.740 are Croats. And then moving across to column 8, 13.851 are Serbs. And actually moving out to column 14, 8.956 are Hungarians. So what that means, Mr. Hadzic, isn't it true that this Beli Manastir that is going to be part of your Serb District --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. May we know, is it the whole page or just a part of the page? Because I don't see Yugoslavs as the option.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's on the next page. That's going to be as page 27 in e-court file. Just so Your Honour knows the census, a single page is spread across two of these pages. The columns continue out and so -- But if I may say, Mr. President, this may be something for re-direct. I've got questions that I'd like to ask Mr. Hadzic, and if my learned friend would like to ask questions about the percentage of people declaring them Yugoslavs there, he is free to do that on his re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, my understanding, the witness is entitled to see the whole document, not just a part of it or just half of the page of this particular document before he -- he could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't see that, Mr. Zivanovic. This is more a technical problem than anything else. If there something in the -- in -- in -- in the question that warrants the entire document to be shown, we'll go to that. But, for the moment, I don't see that. Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've gone the math here, Mr. Hadzic, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment. No, I see why we don't have anything on the English part of the screen. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: They didn't translate the entire -- we do have an English version of the chart with the columns, if Your Honours would like to see that. But just names what are the different nationalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can we agree to this: Out of a total 54.265 people in that municipality, only 13.851, which by my math is about 25 percent, are Serb people. I should say, clarify that, people who declare themselves to be Serb. Twenty-five percent of those living in Beli Manastir are people who declare themselves to be Serb. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, yes, that is the part that declared themselves as such, if the manipulation hadn't already taken place, because the Croatian Democratic Union had already come into power when the census was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, he didn't say the word "Croats." So it should -- maybe he -- he should repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that the Croatian Democratic Union had already taken power by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that -- well, let me put it this way, Mr. Hadzic, just to stay on my question. Beli Manastir, the municipality then that you're asserting was going to be in your Serb District is a place in which Serbs, people who declared themselves to be Serbs, constituted only 25 percent of the population. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that from this census. But I don't know if it was actually so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is no matter how you start drawing lines, it's not going to result in there being a Beli Manastir municipality that's going to be a majority Serb; correct? The fact is the Serbs were a distinct minority in that particular area of the SBWS. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that they were a distinct minority, but they were there in the percentage that you referred to, if the census is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we could scroll down this page we're seeing and look at Osijek. According to my calculations, those declaring themselves Serbs in Osijek municipality are in about 20 per cent of the total population. Does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really deal with these things, but it could be like that, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just so we're clear because we know that as of the 22nd of November, 1991, the Croats, the Croatian side, was still in control of the Osijek town, and the confrontation line actually fell somewhere south of the town, between Osijek and Vukovar. So the Serb side, the Yugoslav side as you put it, did not control Osijek town as of the date of this Law on Territorial Organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law that you are referring to had in its title that it was a provisional, temporary law. The Croatian side was in control of Osijek before, always, even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But we could go back to the law and look at the page on Osijek, and what we're going to see is that in fact the town of Osijek itself is among the places that is going to be a part of the SBWS district; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand it that way. It was written in the former SFRY and in former Croatia. All the municipalities were copied from there including the municipal seat, the town, and all the villages are written there which were not even near the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We can break here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I have just one moment, Mr. President. I've got a technical problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, before we move ahead, I want to give you a -- an opportunity to respond to something that your counsel raised in one of his objections because I don't want you to feel like we're being unfair to you. And this relates to the Yugoslav group on the census. So we could take a moment to look at those numbers as well. I see you have something to say.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is okay now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you get the interpretation of my comments just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could -- we're still with Exhibit P1776, the census, which was tab 394, and you mentioned this in your direct examination and just so that the Chamber can see what you're referring to. We could now go to page 27 of the exhibit, which as we all can see now continues at the top with column number 15. And so this is a continuation out to the right of the heading at the top of the previous page. So here on this page we see more groups referred to, in terms of those declaring their nationality, starting with Germans, Poles, and moving out to column number 29, which relates to Yugoslavs, that as being people who did not declare their nationality. Is that the group that you have referred to when we talk about the demographic data, Mr. Hadzic, is the Yugoslavs there in column 29?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my counsel's objection. That's probably what he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your direct examination, actually, I think you asserted that if you add the number of Yugoslavs to the number of Serbs who resided in Vukovar, then that would put you at 50 per cent, so that's why I'm raising it with you directly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember having said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So just moving back one page to 26, again, looking at Beli Manastir and the number there, a total of 54.265. That's total people who declared and people who did not declare themselves. 22.700 Croats; 13.800 Serbs; 8.900 Hungarians. And then moving to the right, we see that this is row number 13. And then if we move now to page 28 of this document for the continuation, and if we continue to follow row 13 across to the Yugoslav column, then we can see how many Yugoslavs, or people are as down as Yugoslavs, from Beli Manastir. So applying this to Beli Manastir, Mr. Hadzic, would you agree with me that, according to the 1991 census, there were 4.265 Yugoslavs in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, if we are looking at the right column and if the census data is correct. I have to say something for the sake of truth. This census took place before the 22nd of November, 1991, when the decision was drafted, the temporary proposal of the assembly decision. On the 22nd of November, almost all of the towns in our environs were emptied of Serbs basically. If you remember Dzakula's statement, he said that 174 villages were not only emptied of people but destroyed, and most of those people went to the other side independent of me or the government. And especially the towns of Podgorska Slatina, Daruvar, Pakrac, Pozega, those towns were completely emptied of Serbs. If we are to look at these figures objectively, one needs to bear that in mind. The figure would be zero in such columns which depict the number of Serbs in those towns, where now there are 5,000, 6,000 or 10,000 Serbs, on 22 November there were zero Serbs there, and especially in Zagreb there were also no Serbs left. I'm not saying anything against or for it, but just bear that in mind. It was a temporary decision. And in 1995, the houses were still preserved and the Croats could return, and most of them did return to their homes, as opposed to the Serbs who have never returned to Croatian territory to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, looking at this decision you've just referred to, the decision on the territorial organisation, page 90 of the English, and we touched on this just briefly before the break but I want to come back to it now. We're seeing here now Osijek and the towns within the Osijek municipality that are following within the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me give you an exhibit number. It's -- it's L1, tab 388, page 90 of the English, and 31 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So here we see Osijek municipality under item number 5. But if you move down alphabetically, we see that actually Osijek, the town itself, is falling within the terms of this law, but as of 22nd November, the date of this law, Mr. Hadzic, Osijek actually was still in the hands of the Croatian side; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that a few minutes before the last break. It was in the hands of the Croatian side at the time, before that, and even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so what this means is that as of the 22nd of November, 1991, it was the position of the SBWS government that Osijek was not yet -- although Osijek was not yet in your control, it was your intention, or the intention of those on the Serbian side, to take Osijek. This is the territorial aspiration, in other words; correct? You were not finished because you had no taken Osijek?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it's --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct something. In line 25 of the previous page, you said Law on Territorial Organisation but it was a Law on Provisional Territorial Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what was intended is that Osijek, when it was liberated as you would put it, would itself fall within the terms of this law until an overall settlement would be reached with Croatia for the permanent setting of the borders. Is that was -- is that what the intention was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I never heard anyone who was serious enough say that Osijek had to be attacked, liberated, or taken, as you put it. I disagree with that. They simply included the entire five municipalities of the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, Vinkovci, Osijek and Vukovar included. Only the municipality of Vukovar and Beli Manastir were completely in the hands of the district. Osijek was, of course, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You just said here, Mr. Hadzic, that you personally never heard anyone who was serious enough to say that Osijek had to be attacked, liberated, or taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could now move to tab 1048, P1079. It's a video and we will be asking for the interpretation. So we'll wait for them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan: Well, it happened four days ago when we were liberated Borovo Naselje, my units, and I got the sniper. "The reporter: Is it a serious wound? "Arkan: No, it is a light wound and I returned to the front line immediately so I have not even been absent from the front line. "The reporter: There is a hole in the gun as well? "Arkan: Yes, this is the hole. This is how it was. There's a hole, that is the small calibre sniper. It is over and forgotten now. "The reporter: What next? "Arkan: Well, we go on. We go to Osijek. Osijek."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you remember the video? We've played it a lot during the trial of when you and others were at the Velepromet facility on the 20th of November just after the meeting. Do you remember that video?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember being at Velepromet and that there was a private camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you remember the -- the footage that's been shown that shows you, Arkan, other people standing around at Velepromet on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the yard of the Velepromet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you remember that Arkan was wounded at that time? He had this bandage on his hand at that time. Do you remember him being wounded, as is indicated in this video we just saw?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it here, but I don't recall the other footage. I wasn't paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event, you said you weren't aware of anyone advocating taking or liberating Osijek. What this shows is in fact at least one person was doing that, and that was Arkan, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well what I said, and I will repeat: I said that I did not hear of anyone serious enough who was for it, and I did hear hundreds of fools saying that we need to go, I don't even know where. It wasn't only Arkan. There were people causing trouble in the street. There were always people around having such suggestions to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now coming back again, if we could move back to the Law on Temporary -- Temporary Territorial Organisation. We were looking at the places. And you had just mentioned the other municipalities a moment ago before we -- we played the video. Vinkovci was one of those, I believe. You said they simply included the entire five municipalities of the former socialist -- Vinkovci, Osijek and Vukovar included.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a mistake. I had four in mind: Beli Manastir, Vinkovci, Vukovar, and Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you about that, just to get that clarified. Vinkovci, Osijek, Vukovar, and Beli Manastir would be the four that you're -- envisioned would be a part of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you shouldn't say that it was what I envisaged. It was the assembly that envisaged the temporary organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the answer of the witness was not translated correctly. He could repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said when you say "you," you probably don't mean me personally. It was an assembly decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would assume that you endorsed this decision, since it went to the assembly after having been raised by your justice minister, Mr. Susa, during your government meeting on the 19th, however; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government voted on it, and I was only one vote. It was a matter of form. It was to -- to be a temporary solution, leaving the right to decide in the hands of the people. And I don't think, as you believe, that all non-Serbs did not wish to stay in Yugoslavia. I don't think that is true because many people who lived in that country believed it to be a good country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Beli Manastir in the law document that we have, page 87 of the English -- Mr. Hadzic, do you see it on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're not seeing it over here, Mr. President. I don't -- now it's up. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just keeping this in mind, a couple of the places within the municipality, for example, this place called Baranjsko Petrovo Selo; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the first one on the list just below Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And there's a Bilje. That's at the bottom in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just keeping those two in mind as an example, I'd like to now move back to 1776, the census, tab 394, and what I'm getting at here, Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to put to you, you've talked about how, if I may put it this way, the municipalities or the demographic composition was manipulated by the Croatian authorities. What I'm going to put to you here is that the fact is you had individuals of both ethnicities living in the smaller towns and villages and it's simply where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could go to e-court page 34 -- sorry. 03443199. The e-court page is the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Chamber but I did not say that the census was a consequence of manipulation. I said that there was a possibility of manipulation but I do not have information that would confirm any manipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I could assist the Registrar. If you're in e-court and you click on the drop-down menu that gives the page number of the document and then scroll down toward the bottom of the census, you'll start seeing ERN numbers as the actual e-court page number, and that's what I'm referring to. Well, can you find -- sorry. Can the Registrar find it with the ERN -- just referring to the document by ERN number 34 -- 03448199. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you recognise this? This is one of those -- the charts that is attached to the back of the census?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what these do is for each municipality, they give the breakdown in terms of the ethnic composition of the settlements, towns, within the municipality. And so I'm coming to this because if you look at the two places we just spoke about, Baranjsko Petrovo Selo, which is just west of Beli Manastir, the town, we see that's a red place. That's a Croat town. Down toward the bottom of the municipality, Bilje, is also a red spot. And would you agree with me, Mr. Hadzic, that if we went through all the towns in the municipalities here in this temporary law, a good many of them, quite possibly the majority of them, would be red places, red because that's where the Croatian population was in the majority?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree that it was so at the time of the census. But the government I presided over had not provoked the Croatian side to attack Western Slavonia and empty it completely. All those people went to the eastern part of Slavonia. I had no influence over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if we could move to the chart for Osijek, that's at page 0344825A. We can again see the relative ethnicities of the places in that municipality. And just so we know as indicated in the upper left hand of the chart, Mr. Hadzic, a solid circle indicates an absolute majority, whereas, one that is not a solid circle but is just a coloured circle indicates a relative majority; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what that would mean, for example, is that Osijek town is an absolute majority, whereas off to the south-west, Bresce would be a place where there was a relative majority of Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, again, applying this back to the Law on Temporary Territorial Organisation, the plan, the aspiration was to extend your laws and your control, political control, over a place, even Osijek which was just an overwhelmingly Croatian town; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our laws could not be implemented even where we were because it was all the army there. It was the military administration. This was a plan for a future peaceful resolution, something to be discussed. It was not for the law to be implemented. We couldn't even implement the law in Ilok, never mind Osijek, where we weren't even present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if we go to 03448295, we can take look at Ilok and Western Srem. Setting aside the fact, as you claim, that Ilok was under military administration, the fact is, sir, that for you to achieve and the SBWS to achieve political control over a place like Ilok, given its absolute Croatian majority, the only way for you to achieve that would be to remove most of the Croatian people who lived there because they were never going to accept it. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's a question. Is it true that the only way you would have been able to achieve political control over a place like Ilok is by removing all or most of the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the presentation of evidence, you had your own witness who personally admitted that he did that, and I never saw this person in my life, and I had nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm asking you as essentially the political leader of Serbs in Croatia, which is what you were at the time, and wasn't it the policy of your government that it would be necessary to remove all or most of the Croatian people from places, such as Ilok, in order to achieve political control over that territory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my policy or the policy of my government. All we wanted was to remain in Yugoslavia and to achieve our right to self-determination, which we had, pursuant to promises of some ambassadors of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if we could please return to L1, tab 388, back to the Law on Temporary Territorial Organisation. Page 91 of the English. And it should be approximately page 32 of the B/C/S. I want to go to Article 14, Article 14 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you have that, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to correct in line 24, I meant some ambassadors of countries of the United Nations. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Here in Article 14 we have the administration -- the provision that says: "The administrative organ of the municipality is the Executive Council of the municipality, which is assigned by the government of the Serb District."

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before the last break, you indicated that because of the situation, the conflict, et cetera, the Executive Council of the municipality would serve essentially as its government until there could be elections and the formation of a -- a normal government. Is that an acceptable way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood me correctly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving to Article 2 -- excuse me, 22. This provides that: "The administrative organ of a municipality is the Executive Council of the municipality, which is appointed by the Serb District government. "The president and six members of the Executive Council of the municipality are appointed by the decision of the government of the Serb District, which also passes more specific documents regarding their work." Mr. Hadzic, my question is whether you recall actually exercising this authority in your capacity as prime minister, the appointment of people to Executive Councils?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that authority. That authority lay with the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you sign off on government decisions to appoint people to the Executive Council of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a different question. I signed government decisions adopted by the government, but they could also have been signed by the vice-president if I was away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 363, which is L53.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a decision on organising and the way of work of municipal Executive Council, and it is dated 3rd of December, 1991. Do you recall this document? Do you recall this law?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. I remember this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the bottom. It appears that it is a decision of the government that you then signed off on as the president of the government.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see anything of dispute here. If I signed it, yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in Article 2 it says that: "Within the rights and duties of a municipality, the Executive Council answers to the government for the situation in all areas of social life as well as for the application of the established policy, regulations, and general legal document of the National Assembly that direct and co-ordinate the work of municipal... bodies." So by appointing people to these municipal Executive Councils and by having the Executive Council answer to the government, then what this did, Mr. Hadzic, was to ensure that SBWS government policy could now be applied throughout the municipalities through the municipal council -- or excuse me, through the Executive Councils. Is that what was intended here as the structure?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it should have been, so it's some sort of conditional. If conditions are created, then that is how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving to page 2 of the English, Article 10. In this section of the law, we have the relationship of the Executive Council and the government. And then in Article 10 it says that: "The Executive Council has to inform the government about the conduct of the policy that the Executive Council has set ..." And it continues on. And then in Article 12: "Executive Council must act in accordance with the government directions and conclusions passed with regards to the consideration of issues that refer to the work of the Executive Council and especially in relation to the application of the established government policy, law, and other regulations," et cetera. Now, Mr. Hadzic, again, this tell us, does it not, that the Executive Councils were subordinate to the government and the government policy and that they were there to actually ensure that government policy was applied at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 411, L57. Page 73 of the English, 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now here we see -- referring to a session held on the 28th of November, 1991, six days after adoption of the Law on the Provisional Territorial Organisation, which is also referred to in the preamble here, pursuant to that law what's happening here is that the government is appointing a gentleman named Boro Zivanovic of Beli Manastir to be the chairman of the Executive Council. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall signing off on the appointment of Mr. Zivanovic to this position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you did this in Dalj on the 3rd of December?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did it in Erdut. However, the document was drafted in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 282, Exhibit P02161.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a decision published in the Official Gazette of the Beli Manastir municipality from the 18th of October, 1991. So it's before the date of your appointment of Mr. Zivanovic to the chair of the Executive Council. But I did want to talk a little about his activities prior to the time you appointed him to that position. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we move to the next page in B/C/S, please, to correspond to the page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't quite there yet. I wanted to at least ask Mr. Hadzic if we could agree on the name of this decision before we move to paragraph II.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a decision to change street names in the town of Beli Manastir; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving now to the next page of the B/C/S, same page of the English, we can see a list of about 41 street names that are being changed. Can we agree, Mr. Hadzic, that what's essentially happening here is that street names that bear a more Croatian name are being changed to street names that bear more of a Serbian name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. Those people were mostly appointed by the Communist government during the Communist regime. There are Croats, Serbs there, maybe a few more Croats, but there are Serbs too, most of them are the former Yugoslav leaders appointed by the Communist regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the new names -- we don't have to look at them all. There are some names there that appear to be more historical Serbian figures. I see some Serbian duke, some Vojvoda at 14, 15, 16.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Vojvodas from the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this decision is signed by Mr. Zivanovic. How long had you known Mr. Zivanovic before you appointed him to the Executive Council on the 3rd of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Perhaps a couple of months. Maybe even half a year. But I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And he is signing off on these decisions now. This one is from October 18th, a month to the day, actually, prior to the fall of Vukovar. Can we agree that in Beli Manastir, that municipality, or most of it, was under Serb control from quite an early period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree Boro Zivanovic was the president of the Executive Council there even before the government established that. The government just confirmed the factual situation that had existed as of September. He never reported back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could have tab 216, please. Exhibit 2150A.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we see here a decision of -- signed off on by Mr. Borivoje Zivanovic even quite earlier on the 5th of September. And this is a decision on the termination of employment of all persons who openly supported the overthrown regime of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in Article 1 it says, refers to: "A termination of employment of all persons who openly supported the overthrown regime and who, if they remain at their place of employment, would disturb the formal work process or irritate other employees which could lead to serious, specific and political problems, regardless of their ethnic or religious affiliations." Mr. Hadzic, were you aware that from early September Mr. Zivanovic was up in Beli Manastir issuing or adopting legislation like this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. I just told you that he did not report back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you didn't know any of this about him at that time that you appointed him in December, actually, to be formally the head of the municipal council for Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know that. At that time, the government whose president I was had not been established yet. They had their president of the municipality before I became prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you agree with legislation like this that he was passing, that gave them the power to essentially fire people if they might irritate other employees, if they remain at their place of employment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't agree with that. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is that Mr. Zivanovic here was an extremist and he was taking advantage of the Serbian control over Beli Manastir to persecute non-Serbs, Croats, and others who were not accepting of the political change that was now in place. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I've not seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He was an extremist. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that information. However, if he drafted this, I would agree that his way of thinking was rather extremist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into private session for the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of July, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.01 p.m.,
